2 Production

In this chapter we study production in multisector environments. The basic framework is input-output analysis, which was initiated by Wassily Leontief (1905–1999) and popularized in Leontief (1941). Input-output analysis is routinely used to organize national accounts and study inter-industry relationships. In 1973, Leontief received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on input-output systems.

Input-output analysis is currently being incorporated into modern theories of trade, growth, shock propagation and aggregate fluctuations in multisector models (Section 2.4 provides a detailed list of references). One of the reasons for renewed interest is that the introduction of concepts from network analysis and graph theory has yielded new insights. This chapter provides an introduction to the main ideas.

2.1Multisector Models¶

In this section we introduce the basic input output model, explain the network interpretation of the model, and connect traditional questions, such as the relative impact of demand shocks across sectors, to network topology and network centrality.

2.1.1Production Networks¶

We begin with the foundational concepts of input-output tables and how they relate to production networks. To simplify the exposition, we ignore imports and exports in what follows. (References for the general case are discussed in Section 2.4.)

2.1.1.1Input-Output Analysis¶

Agencies tasked with gathering national and regional production accounts (such as the US Bureau of Economic Analysis) compile input-output data based on the structure set out by Leontief (1941). Firms are divided across nnn sectors, each of which produces a single homogeneous good. These sectors are organized into an input-output table, a highly simplified example of which is

sector 1sector 2sector 3
sector 1a11a_{11}a11​a12a_{12}a12​a13a_{13}a13​
sector 2a21a_{21}a21​a22a_{22}a22​a23a_{23}a23​
sector 3a31a_{31}a31​a32a_{32}a32​a33a_{33}a33​

Entries aija_{ij}aij​ are called the input-output coefficients;

aij=value of sector j’s inputs purchased from sector itotal sales of sector j.a_{ij} = \frac{\text{value of sector } j \text{'s inputs purchased from sector } i} {\text{total sales of sector } j}.aij​=total sales of sector jvalue of sector j’s inputs purchased from sector i​.

Thus, aija_{ij}aij​ is large if sector iii is an important supplier of intermediate goods to sector jjj. The sum of the jjj-th column of the table gives the value of all inputs to sector jjj. The iii-th row shows how intensively each sector uses good iii as an intermediate good.

The production coefficient matrix A=(aij)A = (a_{ij})A=(aij​) induces a weighted digraph G=(V,E,w)\gG = (V, E, w)G=(V,E,w), where V=[n]V = \natset{n}V=[n] is the list of sectors and

E:={(i,j)∈V×V:aij>0}E := \setntn{(i, j) \in V \times V}{a_{ij} > 0}E:={(i,j)∈V×V:aij​>0}

is the edge set. The values aija_{ij}aij​ show backward linkages across sectors.

Given i∈Vi \in Vi∈V, the set O(i)\oO(i)O(i) of direct successors of iii is all sectors to which iii supplies a positive quantity of output. The set I(i)\iI(i)I(i) is all sectors that supply a positive quantity to iii.

Figure 2.1 illustrates the weighted digraph associated with the 15 sector version of the input-output tables provided by the Bureau of Economic Analysis for the year 2021.[1] An arrow from iii to jjj indicates a positive weight aija_{ij}aij​. Weights are indicated by the widths of the arrows, which are proportional to the corresponding input-output coefficients. The sector codes are provided in Table 2.1. The size of vertices is proportional to their share of total sales across all sectors.

A quick look at Figure 2.1 shows that manufacturing (ma) is an important supplier for many sectors, including construction (co) and agriculture (ag). Similarly, the financial sector (fi) and professional services (pr) supply services to a broad range of sectors. On the other hand, education (ed) is relatively downstream and only a minor supplier of intermediate goods to other sectors.

The color scheme for the nodes is by hub-based eigenvector centrality, with hotter colors indicating higher centrality. Later, in Section 2.1.3 we will give an interpretation of hub-based eigenvector centrality for this setting that connects to relative impact of demand shocks.

2.1.1.2Connectedness¶

We will gain insights into input-output networks by applying some of the graph-theoretic notions studied in Section 1.4. One elementary property we can investigate is connectedness. We can imagine that demand and productivity shocks diffuse more widely through a given production network when the network is relatively connected. Conversely, the impact of a demand shock occurring within an absorbing set will be isolated to sectors in that set.

The 15 sector network in Figure 2.1 is strongly connected. Checking this visually is hard, so instead we use a graph-theoretic algorithm that finds strongly connected components from QuantEcon’s DiGraph class. (This class is convenient for the current problem because instances are created directly from the adjacency matrix.) Examining the attributes of this class when the weights are given by the 15 sector input-output model confirms its strong connectedness. The same class can be used to verify that the network is also aperiodic. Hence, the input-output matrix AAA is primitive. This fact will be used in computations below.

2.1.1.3Disaggregation¶

Figure 2.2 repeats the graphical representation for the more disaggregated 71 sector case. Sector codes are provided in Table 2.2. Input-output coefficients below 0.010.010.01 were rounded to zero to increase visual clarity. As in the 15 sector case, the size of vertices and edges is proportional to share of sales and input-output coefficients respectively. Hotter colors indicate higher hub-based eigenvector centrality (which we link to propagation of demand shocks in Section 2.1.3).

Unlike the 15 sector case, the 71 sector 2021 input-output matrix is not strongly connected. This is because it contains sinks (sectors with zero out-degree). For example, according to the data, 441 “motor vehicle and parts dealers” do not supply any intermediate inputs, although they do of course supply products to final consumers.

2.1.2Equilibrium¶

Equilibrium in Leontief models involves tracing the impact of final demand as it flows backward through different sectors in the economy. To illustrate the challenges this generates, consider the simplified network shown in Figure 2.3. Suppose sector 3 receives a positive demand shock. Meeting this demand will require greater output from its immediate suppliers, which are sectors 2 and 4. However, an increase in production in sector 2 requires more output from sector 1, which then requires more output from sector 3, where the initial shock occurred. This, in turn, requires more output from sectors 2 and 4, and so on. Thus, the chain of backward linkages leads to an infinite loop. Resolving this tail chasing problem requires some analysis.

All numbers are understood to be in units of national currency—dollars, say. For each sector iii we have the accounting identity

2.1.2.3Assumptions¶

It is common to interpret the expression x∗=(I−A)−1dx^* = (I - A)^{-1} dx∗=(I−A)−1d from (2.6) as meaning that supply is driven by demand. While this is not a universal truth, it does have plausibility in some settings, such as when analyzing demand shifts in the short run. Changes in demand lead to changes in inventories, which typically cause firms to modify production quantities. We investigate these ideas in depth in Section 2.1.3.

Another assumption concerns the production function in each sector. You might recall from elementary microeconomics that the Leontief production function takes the form

x=f(z1,…,zn)=min⁡{γ1z1,…,γnzn}.x = f(z_1, \ldots, z_n) = \min\{ \gamma_1 z_1, \ldots, \gamma_n z_n \}.x=f(z1​,…,zn​)=min{γ1​z1​,…,γn​zn​}.
(2.7)

Here xxx is output in a given sector, {γi}\{\gamma_i\}{γi​} is a set of parameters and {zi}\{z_i\}{zi​} is a set of inputs. To understand why (2.7) is called a Leontief production function, note that by (2.2) we have

xj=zijaijfor all i∈[n] such that aij>0.x_j = \frac{z_{ij}}{a_{ij}} \quad \text{for all } i \in \natset{n} \text{ such that } a_{ij}> 0.xj​=aij​zij​​for all i∈[n] such that aij​>0.
(2.8)

If we interpret z/0=∞z/0 = \inftyz/0=∞ for all z⩾0z \geq 0z⩾0, then (2.8) implies xj=min⁡i∈[n]zij/aijx_j = \min_{i \in \natset{n}} z_{ij}/a_{ij}xj​=mini∈[n]​zij​/aij​. This is a version of (2.7) specialized to sector jjj. Hence (2.7) arises naturally from Leontief input-output analysis.

A final comment on assumptions is that, while the Leontief model is too simple for some purposes, it serves as a useful building block for more sophisticated models. We discuss one such model in Section 2.2.1.

2.1.3Demand Shocks¶

In this section we study impacts of changes in demand via a power series representation ∑i⩾0Ai\sum_{i \geq 0} A^i∑i⩾0​Ai of the Leontief inverse LLL. We assume throughout that r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1, so that the series and LLL are finite and equal.

2.1.3.1Response to Demand Shocks¶

Consider the impact of a demand shock of size Δd\Delta dΔd, so that demand shifts from d0d_0d0​ to d1=d0+Δdd_1 = d_0 + \Delta dd1​=d0​+Δd. The equilibrium output vector shifts from x0=Ld0x_0 = L d_0x0​=Ld0​ to x1=Ld1x_1 = L d_1x1​=Ld1​. Subtracting the first of these equations from the second and expressing the result in terms of differences gives Δx=LΔd\Delta x = L \Delta dΔx=LΔd. Using the geometric sum version of the Leontief inverse yields

Δx=Δd+A(Δd)+A2(Δd)+⋯\Delta x = \Delta d + A (\Delta d) + A^2 (\Delta d) + \cdotsΔx=Δd+A(Δd)+A2(Δd)+⋯
(2.9)

The sums in this term show how the shock propagates backward through the production network:

  1. Δd\Delta dΔd is the initial response in each sector,

  2. A(Δd)A (\Delta d)A(Δd) is the response generated by the first round of backward linkages,

  3. A2(Δd)A^2 (\Delta d)A2(Δd) is the response generated by the second round, and so on.

The total response is the sum of responses at all rounds.

We can summarize the above by stating that a typical element ℓij\ell_{ij}ℓij​ of L=∑m⩾0AmL = \sum_{m \geq 0} A^mL=∑m⩾0​Am shows the total impact on sector iii of a unit change in demand for good jjj, after taking into account all direct and indirect effects. LLL itself is reminiscent of a Keynesian multiplier: changes in demand are multiplied by this matrix to generate final output.

Figure 2.4 helps visualize the Leontief inverse computed from the 15 sector network. Hotter colors indicate larger values for ℓij\ell_{ij}ℓij​, with iii on the vertical axis and jjj on the horizontal axis. We see, for example, that an increase in demand in almost any sector generates a rise in manufacturing output.

2.1.3.2Shock Propagation¶

Figure 2.5 shows the impact of a given vector of demand shocks Δd\Delta dΔd on the 15 sector input-output model. In this simulation, each element of Δd\Delta dΔd was drawn independently from a uniform distribution. The vector Δd\Delta dΔd is shown visually in the panel titled “round 0,” with hotter colors indicating larger values. The shock draw was relatively large in retail (re) and information (in).

The remaining rounds then show the values A2(Δd)A^2 (\Delta d)A2(Δd), A4(Δd)A^4 (\Delta d)A4(Δd), etc., with hotter colors indicating higher values. In each round, to make the within-round comparison between sectors clearer, values of the vector Ai(Δd)A^i (\Delta d)Ai(Δd) are rescaled into the [0,1][0,1][0,1] interval before the color map is applied.

Note that, by round 6, the values of Ai(Δd)A^i (\Delta d)Ai(Δd) have settled into a fixed pattern. (This is only up to a scaling constant, since values are rescaled into [0,1][0,1][0,1] as just discussed.) Manufacturing is the most active sector, while finance and professional services are also quite active. In fact, if we repeat the simulation with a new draw for Δd\Delta dΔd, the pattern of active sectors quickly converges to exactly the same configuration.

We can explain this phenomenon using the Perron–Frobenius theorem. Since AAA is primitive (in the 15 sector case), we know that r(A)−mAmr(A)^{-m} A^mr(A)−mAm converges to eε⊤e \epsilon^\topeε⊤ as m→∞m \to \inftym→∞, where eee and ε\epsilonε are the dominant left and right eigenvectors respectively, normalized so that ⟨ε,e⟩=1\inner{\epsilon, e}=1⟨ε,e⟩=1. It follows that, for large mmm, we have

Am(Δd)≈r(A)m⟨ε,Δd⟩e.A^m (\Delta d) \approx r(A)^m \inner{\epsilon, \Delta d} e.Am(Δd)≈r(A)m⟨ε,Δd⟩e.
(2.10)

In other words, up to a scaling constant, the shock response Am(Δd)A^m (\Delta d)Am(Δd) converges to the dominant right eigenvector, which is also the hub-based eigenvector centrality measure.

In Figure 2.5, the scaling constant is not visible because the values are rescaled to a fixed interval before the color map is applied. However, (2.10) shows us its value, as well as the fact that the scaling constant converges to zero like r(A)mr(A)^mr(A)m. Hence, the dominant eigenpair (r(A),e)(r(A), e)(r(A),e) gives us both the configuration of the response to an arbitrary demand shock and the rate at which the response dies out as we travel back through the linkages.

At this point, we recall that the sectors in Figure 2.1 were colored according to hub-based eigenvector centrality. If you compare this figure to Figure 2.5, you will be above to confirm that, at least for later rounds, the color schemes line up, as predicted by the theory. Finance (fi) and manufacturing (ma) rank highly, as does the professional services sector (pr), which includes consulting, accounting and law.

2.1.3.3Eigenvector Centrality¶

Let’s look at hub-based eigenvector centrality more closely. In a production network, the hub property translates into being an important supplier. Our study of demand shocks in Section 2.1.3 highlighted the significance of the eigenvector measure of hub-based centrality: if sector iii has high rank under this measure, then it becomes active after a large variety of different shocks. Figure 2.6 shows hub-based eigenvector centrality as a bar graph for the 15 sector case. By this measure, manufacturing is by far the most dominant sector in the US economy.

Reviewing the color scheme in Figure 2.2 based on our current understanding of eigenvector centrality, we see that technical servies (54120P), insurance (524), chemical products (325) and primary metals (331) are among the most highly ranked, and hence a wide range of demand shocks generate high activity in these sectors.

To provide some extra context, we show the analogous figure using Australian 2020 input-output data, collected by the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Node size is proportional to sales share and arrow width is proportional to the input-output coefficient. The color map shows hub-based eigenvector centrality.

By this measure, the highest ranked sector is 6901, which is “professional, scientific and technical services.” This includes scientific research, engineering, computer systems design, law, accountancy, advertising, market research, and management consultancy. The next highest sectors are construction and electricity generation.

2.1.3.4Output Multipliers¶

One way to rank sectors that has a long tradition in input-output analysis is via output multipliers. The output multiplier of sector jjj, denoted below by μj\mu_jμj​, is usually defined as the “total sector-wide impact of an extra dollar of demand in sector jjj,” where total means taking into account backward linkages. This measure has historically been of interest to policy makers considering impacts of fiscal stimulus.

Recalling from Section 2.1.3.1 that ℓij\ell_{ij}ℓij​ shows the total impact on sector iii of a unit change in demand for good jjj, we come to the definition

μj=∑i=1nℓij(j∈[n]).\mu_j = \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_{ij} \qquad (j \in \natset{n}).μj​=i=1∑n​ℓij​(j∈[n]).

In vector notation this is μ⊤=1⊤L\mu^\top = \1^\top Lμ⊤=1⊤L or,

μ⊤=1⊤(I−A)−1.\mu^\top = \1^\top (I - A)^{-1}.μ⊤=1⊤(I−A)−1.
(2.11)

Comparing this with (1.39), we see that the vector of output multipliers is equal to the authority-based Katz centrality measure (with the parameter β\betaβ defaulting to unity).

The connection between the two measures makes sense: high authority-based centrality means that a sector has many inward links, and that those links are from other important sectors. Loosely speaking, such a sector is an important buyer of intermediate inputs. A sector highly ranked by this measure that receives a demand shock will cause a large impact on the whole production network.

Figure 2.8 shows the size of output multipiers across 15 US industrial sectors, calculated from the same input-output data as previous 15 sector figures using (2.11). The highest ranks are assigned to manufacturing, agriculture and construction.

2.1.4Forward Linkages¶

Several economic questions connect to relative “upstreamness” of a sector or production good. For example, Olabisi (2020) finds that upstreamness is related to sectoral volatility, while Antràs et al. (2012) examine the relationship between upstreamness and tendency to export. Tariff changes tend to have different aggregate effects when applied to upstream rather than downstream industries Martin & Otto, 2020. Finally, since WWII, many developing countries have systematically supported and encouraged upstream industries Liu, 2019.

In order to study upstreamness, we first introduce the Ghosh model for forward linkages, which uses a rearrangement of terms from the original Leontief model.

2.1.4.1The Ghosh Model¶

Recall that aij=zij/xj=a_{ij}=z_{ij}/x_j =aij​=zij​/xj​= the dollar value of inputs from iii per dollar of sales from jjj. Consider now the related quantities

fij:=zijxi=value of inputs from i to j per dollar output from i.f_{ij} := \frac{z_{ij}}{x_i} = \text{value of inputs from } i \text{ to } j \text{ per dollar output from } i.fij​:=xi​zij​​=value of inputs from i to j per dollar output from i.
(2.12)

Let F:=(fij)i,j∈[n]F := (f_{ij})_{i, j \in \natset{n}}F:=(fij​)i,j∈[n]​. The matrix FFF is called the direct-output matrix or the Ghosh matrix. Element fijf_{ij}fij​ can be interpreted as the size of the “forward linkage” from iii to jjj. Analogous to AAA, the matrix FFF can be viewed as a weight function over output sectors and visualized as in Figure 2.9. This digraph uses the same data source as Figure 2.1.

Let vjv_jvj​ be value added in sector jjj (i.e., payments to factors of production other than intermediate goods). We have

This states that (under perfect competition), the revenue of sector jjj is divided between spending on intermediate goods, which is the first term ∑i=1nzij\sum_{i=1}^n z_{ij}∑i=1n​zij​, and payments to other factors of production (value added).

Using the forward linkages, we can rewrite (2.13) as xj=∑ifijxi+vjx_j = \sum_i f_{ij} x_i + v_jxj​=∑i​fij​xi​+vj​ for all jjj or, in matrix form

x⊤=x⊤F+v⊤.x^\top = x^\top F + v^\top.x⊤=x⊤F+v⊤.
(2.14)

Taking transposes and solving under the assumption r(F)<1r(F) < 1r(F)<1 gives

x∗=(I−F⊤)−1v.x^* = (I - F^\top)^{-1} v.x∗=(I−F⊤)−1v.
(2.15)

We can think of the solution x∗x^*x∗ in (2.15) as the amount of output necessary to acquire a given amount of value added. Since payments of value added are made to underlying factors of production, the Ghosh model is also called a “supply-side input output model”.

Let λ\lambdaλ be an eigenvalue of AAA and let eee be the corresponding eigenvector. Then, for all i∈[n]i \in \natset{n}i∈[n], we have

∑jaijej=λei  ⟺  ∑jzijxjej=λei  ⟺  ∑jfijejxj=λeixi,\sum_j a_{ij} e_j = \lambda e_i \quad \iff \quad \sum_j \frac{z_{ij}}{x_j} e_j = \lambda e_i \quad \iff \quad \sum_j f_{ij} \frac{e_j}{x_j} = \lambda \frac{e_i}{x_i},j∑​aij​ej​=λei​⟺j∑​xj​zij​​ej​=λei​⟺j∑​fij​xj​ej​​=λxi​ei​​,

where we have used the fact that x≫0x \gg 0x≫0. It follows that λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of FFF. The same logic runs in reverse, so AAA and FFF share eigenvalues. Hence r(A)=r(F)r(A)=r(F)r(A)=r(F).

We omit a discussion of the relative merits of supply- and demand-driven input-output models. Our main interest in forward linkages is due to their connection to the topic of ranking sectors by relative upstreamness.

2.1.4.2Upstreamness¶

Which industries are relatively upstream? One proposed measure of upstreamness can be found in Antràs et al. (2012). With fijf_{ij}fij​ as defined in (2.12), the upstreamness uiu_iui​ of sector iii is defined recursively by

ui=1+∑j=1nfijuj.u_i = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^n f_{ij} u_j.ui​=1+j=1∑n​fij​uj​.
(2.16)

The recursive definition of the vector uuu in (2.16) stems from the idea that those sectors selling a large share of their output to upstream industries should be upstream themselves.

We can write (2.16) in vector form as u=1+Fuu = \1 + F uu=1+Fu and solve for uuu as

u=(I−F)−11.u = (I - F)^{-1} \1.u=(I−F)−11.
(2.17)

A unique nonnegativity solution exists provided that r(F)<1r(F) < 1r(F)<1. We expect this to hold in general, due to the findings in Exercise 2.1.7.

Maintaining the convention β=1\beta=1β=1, we see that the upstreamness measure (2.17) proposed by Antràs et al. (2012) is identical to the hub-based Katz centrality measure (1.37) for the production network with weights allocated by the forward linkage matrix FFF.

Figure 2.10 shows the result of computing uuu via (2.17), plotted as a bar graph, for the 15 sector input-output network. Consistent with expectations, the primary commodity producers (agriculture and mining) are the most upstream, while retail and education are typical downstream sectors.

The nodes in Figure 2.9 are also colorized by upstreamness.

2.2General Equilibrium¶

One limitation of the Leontief input-output analysis from Section 2.1 is that demand is fixed and exogenous. In this section we embed Leontief’s model in an equilibrium setting where output and prices are determined by a combination of supply and demand. One objective is to understand how an input-output structure interacts with firm-level shocks to shape aggregate volatility.

2.2.1Supply and Demand¶

Our first step is to introduce and solve a multisector general equilibrium model based on Acemoglu et al. (2012) and Carvalho & Tahbaz-Salehi (2019).

2.2.1.1Production and Prices¶

As in the Leontief economy, there are nnn sectors, also called industries, each of which produces one good. Real output in sector jjj is given by

yj=sjℓjα∏i=1nqijaij.y_j = s_j \ell_j^\alpha \prod_{i=1}^n q_{ij}^{a_{ij}}.yj​=sj​ℓjα​i=1∏n​qijaij​​.
(2.18)

Here

  • sjs_jsj​ is a sector-specific shock (independent across sectors),

  • ℓj\ell_jℓj​ is labor input to sector jjj,

  • qijq_{ij}qij​ is the amount of good iii used in the production of good jjj, and

  • α\alphaα and aija_{ij}aij​ take values in (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) and satisfy α+∑iaij=1\alpha + \sum_i a_{ij}=1α+∑i​aij​=1 for all j∈[n]j \in \natset{n}j∈[n].

The last condition implies constant returns to scale (CRS) in each sector.[2]

2.2.1.2Consumpion¶

Wages are paid to a representative household who chooses consumption to maximize utility ∑iln⁡ci\sum_i \ln c_i∑i​lnci​. In equilibrium, profits are zero, so the only income accruing to the household consists of wage income. The household supplies one unit of labor inelastically. Hence, the budget constraint is ∑ipici=w\sum_i p_i c_i = w∑i​pi​ci​=w.

hi:=piyiw.h_i := \frac{p_i y_i}{w} .hi​:=wpi​yi​​.

2.2.2The Granular Hypothesis¶

We have just constructed a multisector model of production and output. We plan to use this model to study shock propagation and aggregate fluctuations. Before doing so, however, we provide a relatively simple and network-free discussion of shock propagation. The first step is to connect the propagation of shocks to the firm size distribution. Later, in Section 2.2.3, we will see how these ideas relate to the general equilibrium model and the topology of the production network.

2.2.2.1Aggregate vs Idiosyncratic Shocks¶

Some fluctuations in aggregate variables such as GDP growth and the unemployment rate can be tied directly to large exogenous changes in the aggregate environment. One obvious example is the jump in the US unemployment rate from 3.5% to 14.8% between February and April 2020, which was initiated by the onset of the COVID pandemic and resulting economic shutdown.

Other significant fluctuations lack clear macro-level causes. For example, researchers offer mixed explanations for the 1990 US recession, including “technology shocks,” “consumption shocks” and loss of “confidence” Cochrane, 1994. However, these explanations are either difficult to verify on the basis of observable outcomes or require exogenous shifts in variables that should probably be treated as endogenous.

One way to account for at least some of the variability observed in output growth across most countries is on the basis of firm-level and sector-specific productivity and supply shocks. Examples of sector-specific shocks include

  1. the spread of African Swine Fever to China in 2018,

  2. the Great East Japan Earthquake of 2011 and resulting tsunami, which triggered meltdowns at three reactors in the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, and

  3. the destruction of Asahi Kasei Microdevices’ large scale IC factory in Miyazaki Prefecture in October 2020.

In the discussion below, we investigate the extent to which firm-level shocks can drive fluctuations in aggregate productivity.

2.2.2.2The Case of Many Small Firms¶

It has been argued that idiosyncratic, firm-level shocks can account only for a very small fraction of aggregate volatility (see, e.g., Dupor (1999)). The logical heart of this argument is the dampening effect of averaging over independent random variables. To illustrate the main idea, we follow a simple model of production without linkages across firms by Gabaix (2011).

Suppose there are nnn firms, with the size of the iii-th firm, measured by sales, denoted by SiS_iSi​. Since all sales fulfill final demand, GDP is given by Y:=∑i=1nSiY := \sum_{i=1}^n S_iY:=∑i=1n​Si​. We use primes for next period values and Δ\DeltaΔ for first differences (e.g., ΔSi=Si′−Si\Delta S_i = S_i' - S_iΔSi​=Si′​−Si​). We assume that firm growth ΔSi/Si\Delta S_i / S_iΔSi​/Si​ is equal to σFεi\sigma_F \epsilon_iσF​εi​, where {εi}\{\epsilon_i\}{εi​} is a collection of IID random variables corresponding to firm-level idiosyncratic shocks. We also assume that Var⁡(εi)=1\var(\epsilon_i) = 1Var(εi​)=1, so that σF\sigma_FσF​ represents firm-level growth volatility.

GDP growth is then

G:=ΔYY=∑i=1nΔSiY=σF∑i=1nSiYεi.G := \frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \Delta S_i}{Y} = \sigma_F \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{S_i}{Y} \epsilon_i.G:=YΔY​=Y∑i=1n​ΔSi​​=σF​i=1∑n​YSi​​εi​.

Treating the current firm size distribution {Si}\{S_i\}{Si​} and hence GDP as given, show that, under the stated assumptions, the standard deviation of GDP growth σG:=(Var⁡G)1/2\sigma_G := (\var G)^{1/2}σG​:=(VarG)1/2 is

σG=σFHnwhere   Hn:=(∑i=1n(SiY)2)1/2.\sigma_G = \sigma_F H_n \quad \text{where } \; H_n := \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{S_i}{Y} \right)^2 \right)^{1/2}.σG​=σF​Hn​where Hn​:=(i=1∑n​(YSi​​)2)1/2.
(2.26)
Solution to Exercise 2.2.9

This expression follows easily from the definition of variance and the independence of firm-level shocks, which allows us to pass the variance through the sum.

If, say, all firms are equal size, so that nSi=Yn S_i = YnSi​=Y, this means that σG=σF/n\sigma_G = \sigma_F / \sqrt{n}σG​=σF​/n​, so volatility at the aggregate level is very small when the number of firms is large. For example, if the number of firms nnn is 10610^6106, which roughly matches US data, then

σGσF=Hn=(1106)1/2=10−3=0.001.\frac{\sigma_G}{\sigma_F } = H_n = \left( \frac{1}{10^6} \right)^{1/2} = 10^{-3} = 0.001.σF​σG​​=Hn​=(1061​)1/2=10−3=0.001.
(2.27)

Hence firm-level volatility accounts for only 0.1% of aggregate volatility.

To be more concrete, Gabaix (2011) calculates σF=12\sigma_F = 12σF​=12, which means that, by (2.27), σG=0.012\sigma_G = 0.012σG​=0.012%. But the volatility of GDP growth is actually far higher. Indeed, Figure 2.11 reports that, for the US, σG\sigma_GσG​ is approximately 2%2\%2%, which is two orders of magnitude greater. The core message is that, under the stated assumptions, firm-level shocks explain only a tiny part of aggregate volatility.

2.2.2.3The Effect of Heavy Tails¶

There are some obvious problems with the line of reasoning used in Section 2.2.2.2. One is that firms are assumed to be of identical size. In reality, most firms are small to medium, while a relative few are enormous. For example, in the US, a small number of giants dominate technology, electronics and retail.

Gabaix (2011) emphasized that we can get closer to actual GDP volatility by more thoughtful specification of the firm size distribution. Altering the distribution {Si}i=1n\{S_i\}_{i=1}^n{Si​}i=1n​ changes the value HnH_nHn​ in (2.27), which is called the Herfindahl index. This index is often applied to a group of firms in a sector to measure industry concentration. For given aggregate output YYY, the Herfindahl index is minimized when Si=SjS_i = S_jSi​=Sj​ for all i,ji, ji,j. This is the case we considered above. The index is maximized at Hn=1H_n=1Hn​=1 when a single firm dominates all sales. By (2.27), a larger Herfindahl index will increase σG\sigma_GσG​ relative to σF\sigma_FσF​, which allows firm-level shocks to account for more of aggregate volatility.

Calculation of HnH_nHn​ is challenging because the entire firm size distribution {Si}i=1n\{S_i\}_{i=1}^n{Si​}i=1n​ is difficult to observe. Nonetheless, we can estimate HnH_nHn​ by (a) estimating a population probability distribution that fits the empirical distribution {Si}i=1n\{S_i\}_{i=1}^n{Si​}i=1n​ and (b) using analysis or Monte Carlo simulations to calculate typical values of HnH_nHn​.

For step (a), Gabaix (2011) cites the study of Axtell (2001), which finds the firm size distribution to be Pareto with tail index 1.0591.0591.059. If we repeatedly draw {Si}i=1n\{S_i\}_{i=1}^n{Si​}i=1n​ from a Pareto distribution with α=1.059\alpha = 1.059α=1.059 and n=106n=10^6n=106, record the value of HnH_nHn​ after each draw and then take the median value as our estimate, we obtain Hn≈0.88H_n \approx 0.88Hn​≈0.88. In other words, under the Pareto assumption just stated, firm-level volatility accounts for almost 90% of aggregate volatility. In essence, this means that, to explain aggregate volatility, we need to look no further than firm-level shocks.

2.2.2.4Sensitivity Analysis¶

The finding in the previous paragraph is quite striking. How seriously should we take it?

One issue is that the figure Hn≈0.88H_n \approx 0.88Hn​≈0.88 is not robust to small changes in assumptions. For example, the regression in Figure 1.7 suggests that we take 1.321.321.32 as our estimate for the tail index α\alphaα, rather than Axtell’s value of 1.0591.0591.059. If we rerun the same calculation with α=1.32\alpha=1.32α=1.32, the estimated value of HnH_nHn​ falls to 0.0180.0180.018. In other words, firm-level shocks account for only 1.8% of aggregate volatility.

Another issue is that the large value for HnH_nHn​ obtained under Axtell’s parameterization is very sensitive to the parametric family chosen for the firm size distribution. The next exercise illustrates.

  1. for jjj in 1,…,m1, \ldots, m1,…,m do

    1. generate nnn independent draws {Sij}\{S_i^j \}{Sij​} from the LN(μ,σ2)LN(\mu, \sigma^2)LN(μ,σ2) distribution

    2. compute the Herfindahl index HnjH_n^jHnj​ corresponding to {Sij}\{S_i^j \}{Sij​}

  2. end

  3. set HnH_nHn​ equal to the median value of {Hnj}j=1m\{H^j_n\}_{j=1}^m{Hnj​}j=1m​

  4. return HnH_nHn​

2.2.3Network Structure and Shock Propagation¶

The sensitivity analysis in Section 2.2.2.4 suggests we should be skeptical of the claim that firm-level shocks explain most aggregate-level shocks that we observe. This means that either micro-level shocks account for only a small fraction of aggregate volatility or, alternatively, that the model is too simple, and micro-level shocks are amplified through some other mechanism.

An obvious way to explore further is to allow linkages between firms, in the sense that the inputs for some firms are outputs for others. Such an extension opens up the possibility that shocks propagate through the network. This seems plausible even for the sector-specific shocks listed above, such as the Great East Japan Earthquake. Although the initial impact was focused on electricity generation, the flow-on effects for other sectors were rapid and substantial Carvalho et al., 2021.

To investigate more deeply, we connect our discussion of the granular hypothesis back to the multisector models with linkages studied above, allowing us to study flow-on and multiplier effects across industries.

2.2.3.1Industry Concentration and Shocks¶

From (2.25) and the independence of sectoral shocks, the standard deviation σg\sigma_gσg​ of log GDP is given by

σg=σHnwhere   Hn:=(∑i=1nhi2)1/2.\sigma_g = \sigma H_n \quad \text{where } \; H_n := \left( \sum_{i=1}^n h_i^2 \right)^{1/2}.σg​=σHn​where Hn​:=(i=1∑n​hi2​)1/2.
(2.28)

where σ\sigmaσ is the standard deviation of each εi\epsilon_iεi​.

Note that the expression for aggregate volatility takes the same form as (2.26) from our discussion of the granular hypothesis in Section 2.2.2, where HnH_nHn​ was called the Herfindahl index. Once again, this index is the critical determinant of how much firm-level volatility passes through to aggregate volatility. In particular, as discussed in Section 2.2.2.3, independent firm-level shocks cannot explain aggregate volatility unless HnH_nHn​ is large, which in turn requires that the components of the vector hhh are relatively concentrated in a single or small number of sectors.

To investigate an extreme case, we recall from Exercise 2.2.8 that ∑i=1nhi=1/α\sum_{i=1}^n h_i = 1/\alpha∑i=1n​hi​=1/α. The Herfindahl index is Hn:=∥h∥H_n := \| h\|Hn​:=∥h∥, where ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ is the Euclidean norm.

2.2.3.2The Role of Network Topology¶

In the previous section we looked at two extreme cases, neither of which is realistic. Now we look at intermediate cases. In doing so, we note an interesting new feature: unlike the analysis in Section 2.2.2, where the sector shares were chosen from some fixed distribution, the Herfindahl index is now determined by the network structure of production.

To see this, we can use the results of Exercise 2.2.7 to obtain

h=1nL1=1n∑m⩾0Am1.h = \frac{1}{n} L \1 = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{m \geq 0} A^m \1.h=n1​L1=n1​m⩾0∑​Am1.

Recalling our discussion in Section 1.4.3.5, we see that the vector of Domar weights is just a rescaling of the vector of hub-based Katz centrality rankings for the input-output matrix. Thus, the propagation of sector-specific productivity shocks up to the aggregate level depends on the distribution of Katz centrality across sectors. The more “unequal” is this distribution, the larger is the pass through.

Figure 2.13 shows some examples of different network configurations, each of which is associated with a different Katz centrality vector. Not surprisingly, the symmetric network has a constant centrality vector, so that all sectors have equal centrality. This is the maximum diversification case, as discussed in Section 2.2.3.1. The other two cases have nonconstant centrality vectors and hence greater aggregate volatility.[5]

Exercise 2.2.13

Let the nonzero input output coefficient aija_{ij}aij​ shown by arrows in Figure 2.13 all have equal value 0.20.20.2. Show computationally that the hub-based Katz centrality vectors for the hub and star networks are

κh=(1.8,1,1,1,1)andκs=(1.2,1.2,1.2,1.2,1)\kappa_h = (1.8, 1, 1, 1, 1) \quad \text{and} \quad \kappa_s = (1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1)κh​=(1.8,1,1,1,1)andκs​=(1.2,1.2,1.2,1.2,1)

respectively (for nodes 1,…,51, \ldots, 51,…,5).

The results of Exercise 2.2.13 show that the hub network has the more unequal Katz centrality vector. Not surprisingly, the source node in the hub has a high hub-based centrality ranking. Productivity shocks affecting this sector have a large effect on aggregate GDP.

Figure 2.14 shows hub-based Katz centrality computed from the 15 sector input-output data for 2021. We can see that productivity shocks in manufacturing will have a significantly larger impact on aggregate output than shocks in say, retail or education.

2.2.3.3Supply Shocks vs Demand Shocks¶

In the previous section we saw that the degree to which a productivity shock propagates through the economy depends on the hub-based centrality ranking of the relevant sector. This is intuitive. Sectors that act like hubs supply many sectors, so changes in productivity in these sectors will have large flow-on effects.

This is in contrast with what we learned in Section 2.1.3.4, where a high authority-based centrality measure lead to high shock propagation. The difference can be explained by the source of the shocks: in Section 2.1.3.4, we were concerned with the impact of demand shocks. Demand shocks to sector iii have large flow-on effects when many sectors purchase inputs from sector iii. Hence authority-based centrality measures are appropriate for studying this case.

2.3More Spectral Theory¶

This is a relatively technical section, which analyzes aspects of vector dynamics and spectral theory in more depth. It is aimed at readers who are interested in further mathematical discussion of the theory treated above. The ideas studied here are applied to production problems to generate additional insights into existence and uniqueness of equilibria, as well as later topics such as convergence of distributions for Markov models on networks.

2.3.1Vector Norms¶

In this section we learn about abstract vector norms on Rn\RR^nRn and provide several examples. Later we will see how the different norms are related and how they can be useful for some kinds of network analysis.

2.3.1.1Norms¶

A function ∥⋅∥ ⁣:Rn→R\| \cdot \| \colon \RR^n \to \RR∥⋅∥:Rn→R is called a norm on Rn\RR^nRn if, for any α∈R\alpha \in \RRα∈R and u,v∈Rnu, v \in \RR^nu,v∈Rn,

  1. ∥u∥⩾0\| u \| \geq 0∥u∥⩾0

  2. ∥u∥=0  ⟺  u=0\| u \| =0 \iff u=0∥u∥=0⟺u=0

  3. ∥αu∥=∣α∣∥u∥\| \alpha u \| = |\alpha| \| u\|∥αu∥=∣α∣∥u∥ and

  4. ∥u+v∥⩽∥u∥+∥v∥\| u + v \| \leq \| u \| + \| v \|∥u+v∥⩽∥u∥+∥v∥

(nonnegativity)

(positive definiteness)

(positive homogeneity)

(triangle inequality)

The Euclidean norm is a norm on Rn\RR^nRn, as suggested by its name.

Example 2.3.1.

The ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm of a vector u∈Rnu \in \RR^nu∈Rn is defined by

u=(u1,…,un)↦∥u∥1:=∑i=1n∣ui∣.u = (u_1, \ldots, u_n) \mapsto \| u \|_1 := \sum_{i=1}^n |u_i|.u=(u1​,…,un​)↦∥u∥1​:=i=1∑n​∣ui​∣.
(2.29)

In machine learning applications, ∥⋅∥1\| \cdot \|_1∥⋅∥1​ is sometimes called the “Manhattan norm,” and d1(u,v):=∥u−v∥1d_1 (u, v) := \| u - v \|_1d1​(u,v):=∥u−v∥1​ is called the “Manhattan distance” or “taxicab distance” between vectors uuu and vvv. We will refer to it more simply as the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ distance or ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ deviation.

The ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm and the Euclidean norm are special cases of the so-called ℓp\ell_pℓp​ norm, which is defined for p⩾1p \geq 1p⩾1 by

u=(u1,…,un)↦∥u∥p:=(∑i=1n∣ui∣p)1/p.u = (u_1, \ldots, u_n) \mapsto \| u \|_p := \left( \sum_{i=1}^n |u_i|^p \right)^{1/p}.u=(u1​,…,un​)↦∥u∥p​:=(i=1∑n​∣ui​∣p)1/p.
(2.30)

It can be shown that u↦∥u∥pu \mapsto \| u \|_pu↦∥u∥p​ is a norm for all p⩾1p \geq 1p⩾1, as suggested by the name (see, e.g., Kreyszig (1978)). For this norm, the subadditivity in (d) is called Minkowski’s inequality.

Since the Euclidean case is obtained by setting p=2p=2p=2, the Euclidean norm is also called the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ norm, and we write ∥⋅∥2\| \cdot \|_2∥⋅∥2​ rather than ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ when extra clarity is required.

2.3.1.2Equivalence of Vector Norms¶

When uuu and (um):=(um)m∈N(u_m) := (u_m)_{m \in \NN}(um​):=(um​)m∈N​ are all elements of Rn\RR^nRn, we say that (um)(u_m)(um​) converges to uuu and write um→uu_m \to uum​→u if

∥um−u∥→0 as m→∞ for some norm ∥⋅∥ on Rn.\| u_m - u \| \to 0 \text{ as } m \to \infty \text{ for some norm } \| \cdot \| \text{ on } \RR^n.∥um​−u∥→0 as m→∞ for some norm ∥⋅∥ on Rn.

It might seem that this definition is imprecise. Don’t we need to clarify that the convergence is with respect to a particular norm?

In fact we do not. This is because any two norms ∥⋅∥a\| \cdot \|_a∥⋅∥a​ and ∥⋅∥b\| \cdot \|_b∥⋅∥b​ on Rn\RR^nRn are equivalent, in the sense that there exist finite constants M,NM, NM,N such that

M∥u∥a⩽∥u∥b⩽N∥u∥afor all u∈Rn.M \|u\|_a \leq \| u\|_b \leq N \| u \|_a \quad \text{for all } u \in \RR^n.M∥u∥a​⩽∥u∥b​⩽N∥u∥a​for all u∈Rn.
(2.31)

Fix (um)⊂Rn(u_m) \subset \RR^n(um​)⊂Rn, u∈Rnu \in \RR^nu∈Rn and norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ on Rn\RR^nRn. Taking m→∞m \to \inftym→∞, the following statements are equivalent:

2.3.2Matrix Norms¶

In some applications, the number of vertices nnn of a given digraph is measured in millions or billions. This means that the adjacency matrix AAA is enormous. To control complexity, AAA must often be replaced by a sparse approximation AsA_sAs​. It is natural to require that AAA and AsA_sAs​ are close. But how should we define this?

More generally, how can we impose a metric on the set of matrices to determine similarity or distance between them? One option is to follow the example of vectors on Rn\RR^nRn and introduce a norm on Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k. With such a norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ in hand, we can regard AAA and AsA_sAs​ as close when ∥A−As∥\| A - A_s \|∥A−As​∥ is small.

For this and other reasons, we now introduce the notion of a matrix norm.

2.3.2.1Definition¶

Analogous to vectors on Rn\RR^nRn, we will call a function ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ from Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k to R+\RR_+R+​ a norm if for any A,B∈Mn×kA, B \in \matset{n}{k}A,B∈Mn×k,

  1. ∥A∥⩾0\| A \| \geq 0∥A∥⩾0

  2. ∥A∥=0  ⟺  u=0\| A \| =0 \iff u=0∥A∥=0⟺u=0

  3. ∥αA∥=∣α∣∥A∥\| \alpha A \| = |\alpha| \| A\|∥αA∥=∣α∣∥A∥ and

  4. ∥A+B∥⩽∥A∥+∥B∥\| A + B \| \leq \| A \| + \| B \|∥A+B∥⩽∥A∥+∥B∥

(nonnegativity)

(positive definiteness)

(positive homogeneity)

(triangle inequality)

The distance between two matrices A,BA, BA,B is then specified as ∥A−B∥\| A - B \|∥A−B∥.

Unlike vectors, matrices have a product operation defined over all conformable matrix pairs. We want matrix norms to interact with this product in a predictable way. For example, it is helpful for analysis when a matrix norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ is submultiplicative, meaning that

∥AB∥⩽∥A∥⋅∥B∥     for all conformable matrices A,B.\| A B \| \leq \| A \| \cdot \| B \| \;\; \text{ for all conformable matrices } A, B.∥AB∥⩽∥A∥⋅∥B∥ for all conformable matrices A,B.
(2.32)

A useful implication of (2.32) is that ∥Ai∥⩽∥A∥i\|A^i\| \leq \|A \|^i∥Ai∥⩽∥A∥i for any i∈Ni \in \NNi∈N and A∈Mn×nA \in \matset{n}{n}A∈Mn×n, where AiA^iAi is the iii-th power of AAA.

2.3.2.2The Frobenius Norm¶

One way to construct a norm on matrix space Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k is to first introduce the Frobenius inner product of matrices A=(aij),B=(bij)A = (a_{ij}), B=(b_{ij})A=(aij​),B=(bij​) as

⟨A,B⟩F:=∑i=1n∑j=1naijbij=trace⁡(AB⊤)=trace⁡(BA⊤).\inner{A, B}_F := \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} b_{ij} = \trace(A B^\top) = \trace(B A^\top).⟨A,B⟩F​:=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​aij​bij​=trace(AB⊤)=trace(BA⊤).
(2.33)

From this inner product, the Frobenius norm of A∈Mn×kA \in \matset{n}{k}A∈Mn×k is defined as

∥A∥F:=⟨A,A⟩F1/2.\| A \|_F := \inner{A, A}^{1/2}_F .∥A∥F​:=⟨A,A⟩F1/2​.
(2.34)

In essence, the Frobenius norm converts an n×kn \times kn×k matrix into an nknknk vector and computes the Euclidean norm.

The Frobenius norm is submultiplicative. The next exercise asks you to prove this in one special case.

Exercise 2.3.8

Suppose that AAA is a row vector and BBB is a column vector. Show that (2.32) holds in this case when ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ is the Frobenius norm.

Solution to Exercise 2.3.8

The Frobenius norm reduces to the Euclidean norm for column and row vectors, so (2.32) requires that ∣⟨A,B⟩F∣⩽∥A∥F∥B∥F| \inner{A, B}_F| \leq \| A \|_F \|B\|_F∣⟨A,B⟩F​∣⩽∥A∥F​∥B∥F​. This bound certainly holds: it is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

2.3.2.3The Operator Norm¶

Another important matrix norm is the operator norm, defined at A∈Mn×kA \in \matset{n}{k}A∈Mn×k by

∥A∥:=sup⁡{∥Au∥:u∈Rk and ∥u∥=1},\| A \| := \sup \setntn{ \| A u \| }{ u \in \RR^k \text{ and } \| u \| = 1},∥A∥:=sup{∥Au∥:u∈Rk and ∥u∥=1},
(2.35)

where the norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ on the right hand size of (2.35) is the Euclidean norm on Rn\RR^nRn.

Example 2.3.2.

If A=diag⁡(ai)A = \diag(a_i)A=diag(ai​), then, for any u∈Rnu \in \RR^nu∈Rn we have ∥Au∥2=∑i(aiui)2\|Au\|^2 = \sum_i (a_i u_i)^2∥Au∥2=∑i​(ai​ui​)2. To maximize this value subject to ∑iui2=1\sum_i u_i^2 = 1∑i​ui2​=1, we pick jjj such that aj2⩾ai2a_j^2 \geq a_i^2aj2​⩾ai2​ for all iii and set ui=1{i=j}u_i = \1\{i=j\}ui​=1{i=j}. The maximized value of ∥Au∥\| Au\|∥Au∥ is then

∥A∥=aj2=max⁡i∈[n] ∣ai∣.\| A\| = \sqrt{a_j^2} = \max_{i \in \natset{n}} \, |a_i|.∥A∥=aj2​​=i∈[n]max​∣ai​∣.

2.3.2.4Other Matrix Norms¶

Two other useful matrix norms are the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ and ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ norms given by

∥A∥1:=∑i=1n∑j=1k∣aij∣and∥A∥∞:=max⁡i∈[n], j∈[k]∣aij∣.\| A \|_1 := \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^k |a_{ij}| \quad \text{and} \quad \| A \|_\infty := \max_{i \in \natset{n}, \, j \in \natset{k}} |a_{ij}|.∥A∥1​:=i=1∑n​j=1∑k​∣aij​∣and∥A∥∞​:=i∈[n],j∈[k]max​∣aij​∣.

Prove that both are norms on Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k.

Prove that both norms are submultiplicative.

2.3.2.5Equivalence of Matrix Norms¶

In Section 2.3.1.2 we saw that all norms on Rn\RR^nRn are equivalent. Exactly the same result holds true for matrix norms: any two norms ∥⋅∥a\| \cdot \|_a∥⋅∥a​ and ∥⋅∥b\| \cdot \|_b∥⋅∥b​ on Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k are equivalent, in the sense that there exist finite constants M,NM, NM,N such that

M∥A∥a⩽∥A∥b⩽N∥A∥afor all A∈Mn×k.M \|A\|_a \leq \| A\|_b \leq N \| A \|_a \quad \text{for all } A \in \matset{n}{k}.M∥A∥a​⩽∥A∥b​⩽N∥A∥a​for all A∈Mn×k.
(2.37)

A proof can be found (for abstract finite-dimensional vector space) in Bollobás (1999).

Analogous to the vector case, given AAA and (Am):=(Am)m∈N(A_m) := (A_m)_{m \in \NN}(Am​):=(Am​)m∈N​ in Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k, we say that (Am)(A_m)(Am​) converges to AAA and write Am→AA_m \to AAm​→A if ∥Am−A∥→0\| A_m - A \| \to 0∥Am​−A∥→0 as m→∞m \to \inftym→∞, where ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ is a matrix norm. Once again, we do not need to clarify the norm due to the equivalence property. Also, norm convergence is equivalent to pointwise convergence:

Exercise 2.3.14

Prove that, given AAA and (Am)(A_m)(Am​) in Mn×k\matset{n}{k}Mn×k, we have Am→AA_m \to AAm​→A as m→∞m \to \inftym→∞ if and only if every element aijma_{ij}^maijm​ of AmA_mAm​ converges to the corresponding element aija_{ij}aij​ of AAA.

Exercise 2.3.15

Prove the following result for matrices A,B,CA, B, CA,B,C and matrix sequences (Am),(Bm)(A_m), (B_m)(Am​),(Bm​), taking m→∞m \to \inftym→∞ and assuming sizes are conformable:

  1. If Bm→AB_m \to ABm​→A and Am−Bm→0A_m - B_m \to 0Am​−Bm​→0, then Am→AA_m \to AAm​→A.

  2. If Am→AA_m \to AAm​→A, then BAmC→BACB A_m C \to B A CBAm​C→BAC.

Solution to Exercise 2.3.15

Let (Am)(A_m)(Am​) and (Bm)(B_m)(Bm​) have the stated properties. Regarding (i), we use the triangle inequality to obtain

∥Am−A∥=∥Am−Bm+Bm−A∥⩽∥Am−Bm∥+∥Bm−A∥.\| A_m - A \| = \| A_m - B_m + B_m - A \| \leq \| A_m - B_m \| + \| B_m - A \|.∥Am​−A∥=∥Am​−Bm​+Bm​−A∥⩽∥Am​−Bm​∥+∥Bm​−A∥.

Both terms on the right converge to zero, which completes the proof.

Regarding (ii), we use the submultiplicative property to obtain ∥BAmC−BAC∥⩽∥B∥∥Am−A∥∥C∥→0\| B A_m C - B A C \| \leq \| B \| \| A_m - A \| \| C \| \to 0∥BAm​C−BAC∥⩽∥B∥∥Am​−A∥∥C∥→0.

Example 2.3.3.

Convergence of the Perron projection in (1.11) of the Perron–Frobenius theorem was defined using pointwise convergence. By Exercise 2.3.14, norm convergence also holds. One of the advantages of working with norms is that we can give rates of convergence for norm deviation. This idea is discussed further in Section 2.3.3.3.

2.3.3Iteration in Matrix Space¶

Results such as Proposition 1.4.2 already showed us the significance of powers of adjacency matrices. The Perron-Frobenius theorem revealed connections between spectral radii, dominant eigenvectors and powers of positive matrices. In this section we investigate powers of matrices in more depth.

2.3.3.1Gelfand’s Formula¶

One very general connection between matrix powers and spectral radii is Gelfand’s formula for the spectral radius:

Theorem 2.3.2.

For any matrix norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ and A∈Mn×nA \in \matset{n}{n}A∈Mn×n, we have

r(A)=lim⁡k→∞∥Ak∥1/k.r(A) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \| A^k \|^{1/k}.r(A)=k→∞lim​∥Ak∥1/k.
(2.38)

Proofs can be found in Bollobás (1999) or Kreyszig (1978).

Exercise 2.3.17

The references above show that the limit (2.38) always exists. Using this fact, prove that every choice of norm over Mn×n\matset{n}{n}Mn×n yields the same value for this limit.

Solution to Exercise 2.3.17

Let ∥⋅∥a\| \cdot \|_a∥⋅∥a​ and ∥⋅∥b\| \cdot \|_b∥⋅∥b​ be two norms on Mn×n\matset{n}{n}Mn×n. By the results in Section 2.3.2.5, these norms are equivalent, so there exist constants M,NM, NM,N such that ∥Ak∥a⩽M∥Ak∥b⩽N∥Ak∥a\|A^k \|_a \leq M \| A^k \|_b \leq N \| A^k \|_a∥Ak∥a​⩽M∥Ak∥b​⩽N∥Ak∥a​ for all k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N.

∴∥Ak∥a1/k⩽M1/k∥Ak∥b1/k⩽N1/k∥Ak∥a1/k\fore \|A^k \|_a^{1/k} \leq M^{1/k} \| A^k \|_b^{1/k} \leq N^{1/k} \| A^k \|_a^{1/k}∴∥Ak∥a1/k​⩽M1/k∥Ak∥b1/k​⩽N1/k∥Ak∥a1/k​

for all k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N. Taking k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞, we see that the definition of the spectral radius is independent of the choice of norm.

The next exercise shows that r(A)<1r(A)<1r(A)<1 implies ∥Ak∥→0\|A^k\| \to 0∥Ak∥→0 at a geometric rate.

Using (2.38), show that r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 implies the existence of a constant δ<1\delta < 1δ<1 and an M<∞M < \inftyM<∞ such that ∥Ak∥⩽δkM\| A^k \| \leq \delta^k M∥Ak∥⩽δkM for all k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N.

2.3.3.2A Local Spectral Radius Theorem¶

The next theorem is a “local” version of Gelfand’s formula that relies on positivity. It replaces matrix norms with vector norms, which are easier to compute.

Theorem 2.3.3.

Fix A∈Mn×nA \in \matset{n}{n}A∈Mn×n and let ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ be any norm on Rn\RR^nRn. If A⩾0A \geq 0A⩾0 and x≫0x \gg 0x≫0, then

∥Amx∥1/m→r(A)(m→∞).\| A^m x\|^{1/m} \to r(A) \qquad (m \to \infty).∥Amx∥1/m→r(A)(m→∞).
(2.39)

Theorem 2.3.3 tells us that, eventually, for any positive xxx, the norm of the vector AmxA^m xAmx grows at rate r(A)r(A)r(A). A proof can be found in Krasnoselskii (1964).[6]

Example 2.3.4.

In Section 2.1.3 we studied how the impact of a given demand shock Δd\Delta dΔd flows backward through a production network, with Am(Δd)A^m (\Delta d)Am(Δd) giving the impact on sectors at mmm steps (backward linkages). When Δd≫0\Delta d \gg 0Δd≫0 and r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1, Theorem 2.3.3 tells us that ∥AmΔd∥=O(r(A)m)\| A^m \Delta d\| = O(r(A)^m)∥AmΔd∥=O(r(A)m). If we set the norm to ∥⋅∥∞\| \cdot \|_\infty∥⋅∥∞​, this tells us that the maximal impact of demand shocks through backward linkages fades at rate r(A)r(A)r(A).

Solution to Exercise 2.3.21

Let ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ be a norm on Rn\RR^nRn. From the Perron–Frobenius theorem (Theorem 1.2.6), when AAA is primitive, ∥r(A)−mAmx∥→c\| r(A)^{-m} A^m x \| \to c∥r(A)−mAmx∥→c as m→∞m \to \inftym→∞, where c>0c > 0c>0 whenever x≫0x \gg 0x≫0. Hence lim⁡m→∞∥Amx∥1/m=lim⁡m→∞r(A)c1/m=r(A)\lim_{m \to \infty} \| A^m x \|^{1/m} = \lim_{m \to \infty} r(A) c^{1/m} = r(A)limm→∞​∥Amx∥1/m=limm→∞​r(A)c1/m=r(A).

2.3.3.3Convergence to the Perron Projection¶

The local spectral radius theorem assumes A⩾0A \geq 0A⩾0. Now we further strengthen this assumption by requiring that AAA is primitive. In this case, r(A)−mAmr(A)^{-m} A^mr(A)−mAm converges to the Perron projection as m→∞m \to \inftym→∞ (see (1.11)). We want rates of convergence in high-dimensional settings.

We fix A∈Mn×nA \in \matset{n}{n}A∈Mn×n and label the eigenvalues so that ∣λi+1∣⩽∣λi∣|\lambda_{i+1}| \leq |\lambda_i|∣λi+1​∣⩽∣λi​∣ for all iii. Note that ∣λ1∣=λ1=r(A)|\lambda_1| = \lambda_1 = r(A)∣λ1​∣=λ1​=r(A). Let E:=e ε⊤E := e \, \epsilon^\topE:=eε⊤ be the Perron projection.

Proposition 2.3.4.

If AAA is diagonalizable and primitive, then α:=∣λ2/λ1∣<1\alpha := |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| < 1α:=∣λ2​/λ1​∣<1 and

∥r(A)−mAm−E∥=O(αm).\| r(A)^{-m} A^m - E \| = O \left( \alpha^m \right).∥r(A)−mAm−E∥=O(αm).
(2.40)

Thus, an upper bound on the rate of convergence to the Perron projection is determined by the modulus of the ratio of the first two eigenvalues.

Proof.

We saw in (1.5) that Am=∑i=1nλimeiεi⊤A^m = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i^m e_i \epsilon_i^\topAm=∑i=1n​λim​ei​εi⊤​ for all m∈Nm \in \NNm∈N. From this spectral representation we obtain

r(A)−mAm−e1 ε1⊤=r(A)−m(Am−r(A)me1 ε1⊤)=∑i=2nθimeiεi⊤r(A)^{-m} A^m - e_1 \, \epsilon_1^\top = r(A)^{-m} \left( A^m - r(A)^m e_1 \, \epsilon_1^\top \right) = \sum_{i=2}^n \theta_i^m e_i \epsilon_i^\topr(A)−mAm−e1​ε1⊤​=r(A)−m(Am−r(A)me1​ε1⊤​)=i=2∑n​θim​ei​εi⊤​

when θi:=λi/r(A)\theta_i := \lambda_i/r(A)θi​:=λi​/r(A). Let ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ be the operator norm on Mn×n\matset{n}{n}Mn×n. The triangle inequality gives

∥r(A)−mAm−e1 ε1⊤∥⩽∑i=2n∣θi∣m∥eiεi⊤∥⩽∣θ2∣m∑i=2n∥eiεi⊤∥.\| r(A)^{-m} A^m - e_1 \, \epsilon_1^\top \| \leq \sum_{i=2}^n | \theta_i| ^m \| e_i \epsilon_i^\top \| \leq | \theta_2| ^m \sum_{i=2}^n \| e_i \epsilon_i^\top \|.∥r(A)−mAm−e1​ε1⊤​∥⩽i=2∑n​∣θi​∣m∥ei​εi⊤​∥⩽∣θ2​∣mi=2∑n​∥ei​εi⊤​∥.

Since AAA is primitive, the Perron–Frobenius theorem tells us that ∣λ2∣<r(A)|\lambda_2| < r(A)∣λ2​∣<r(A). Hence α:=∣θ2∣<1\alpha := |\theta_2| < 1α:=∣θ2​∣<1. The proof is now complete. ◻

2.3.4Exact Stability Conditions¶

The Neumann series lemma tells us that the linear system x=Ax+dx = Ax + dx=Ax+d has a unique solution whenever r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1. We also saw that, in the input-output model, where AAA is the adjacency matrix, the condition r(A)<1r(A)<1r(A)<1 holds whenever every sector has positive value added (Assumption 2.1.1 and Exercise 2.1.2). Hence we have sufficient conditions for stability.

This analysis, while important, leaves open the question of how tight the conditions are and what happens when they fail. For example, we might ask

  1. To obtain r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1, is it necessary that each sector has positive value added? Or can we obtain the same result under weaker conditions?

  2. What happens when r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 fails? Do we always lose existence of a solution, or uniqueness, or both?

In Section 2.3.4.1 and Section 2.3.4.2 below we address these two questions.

2.3.4.1Spectral Radii of Substochastic Matrices¶

To reiterate, the results in Section 5.1.3 relied on the assumption that every sector has positive value added, which in turn gave us the property r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 for the adjacency matrix of the input-output production network. Positive value added in every sector is not necessary, however. Here we investigate a weaker condition that is exactly necessary and sufficient for r(A)<1r(A)<1r(A)<1. This weaker condition is very helpful for understanding other kinds of networks too, including financial networks, as discussed in Section 5.2.

To begin, recall that a matrix P∈Mn×nP \in \matset{n}{n}P∈Mn×n is called stochastic if P⩾0P \geq 0P⩾0 and P1=1P \1 = \1P1=1. Similarly, P∈Mn×nP \in \matset{n}{n}P∈Mn×n is called substochastic if P⩾0P \geq 0P⩾0 and P1⩽1P \1 \leq \1P1⩽1. Thus, a substochastic matrix is a nonnegative matrix with less than unit row sums. Clearly the transpose Q⊤Q^\topQ⊤ of a nonnegative matrix QQQ is substochastic if and only if QQQ has less than unit column sums.

A natural example of a substochastic matrix is the transpose A⊤A^\topA⊤ of an adjacency matrix AAA of an input-output network. Indeed, such an AAA is nonnegative and, for jjj-th column sum we have

∑iaij=∑izijxj=spending on inputs by sector jtotal sales of sector j.\sum_i a_{ij} = \frac{\sum_i z_{ij}}{x_j} = \frac{\text{spending on inputs by sector } j}{\text{total sales of sector } j}.i∑​aij​=xj​∑i​zij​​=total sales of sector jspending on inputs by sector j​.

Hence ∑iaij⩽1\sum_i a_{ij} \leq 1∑i​aij​⩽1, which says that spending on intermediate goods and services by a given industry does not exceed total sales revenue, is a necessary condition for nonnegative profits in sector jjj. When this holds for all jjj, the adjacency matrix has less than unit column sums.

From Lemma 1.2.7, we see that any substochastic matrix PPP has

r(P)⩽max⁡irowsum⁡i(P)⩽1.r(P) \leq \max_i \rsum_i(P) \leq 1.r(P)⩽imax​rowsumi​(P)⩽1.
(2.41)

We wish to know when we can tighten this to r(P)<1r(P) < 1r(P)<1.

From (2.41), one obvious sufficient condition is that rowsum⁡i(P)<1\rsum_i(P) < 1rowsumi​(P)<1 for all iii. This is, in essence, how we used Assumption 2.1.1 (every sector has positive value added) in the input-output model. Under that condition we have ∑iaij<1\sum_i a_{ij} < 1∑i​aij​<1 for all jjj, which says all column sums are strictly less than one. Hence

max⁡icolsum⁡i(A)<1    ⟺    max⁡irowsum⁡i(A⊤)<1    ⟹    r(A⊤)<1    ⟺    r(A)<1,\max_i \csum_i(A) < 1 \; \iff \; \max_i \rsum_i(A^\top) < 1 \; \implies \; r(A^\top) < 1 \; \iff \; r(A) < 1,imax​colsumi​(A)<1⟺imax​rowsumi​(A⊤)<1⟹r(A⊤)<1⟺r(A)<1,

where the middle implication is by (2.41) and the last equivalence is by r(A)=r(A⊤)r(A)=r(A^\top)r(A)=r(A⊤).

Now we provide a weaker—in fact necessary and sufficient—condition for r(P)<1r(P)<1r(P)<1, based on network structure. To do so, we define an n×nn \times nn×n substochastic matrix P=(pij)P = (p_{ij})P=(pij​) to be weakly chained substochastic if, for all m∈[n]m \in \natset{n}m∈[n], there exists an i∈[n]i \in \natset{n}i∈[n] such that m→im \to im→i and ∑jpij<1\sum_j p_{ij} < 1∑j​pij​<1. Here accessibility of iii from mmm is in terms of the induced weighted digraph.[7]

Exercise 2.3.22

Let A=(aij)∈Mn×nA = (a_{ij}) \in \matset{n}{n}A=(aij​)∈Mn×n be nonnegative. Show that A⊤A^\topA⊤ is weakly chained substochastic if and only if AAA has less than unit column sums and, for each m∈[n]m \in \natset{n}m∈[n], there exists an i∈[n]i \in \natset{n}i∈[n] such that i→mi \to mi→m under (the digraph induced by) AAA and ∑kaki<1\sum_k a_{ki} < 1∑k​aki​<1.

Solution to Exercise 2.3.22

We prove only that the stated conditions on AAA imply that A⊤A^\topA⊤ is weakly chained substochastic, since the proof of the reverse implication is very similar. We set aij′:=ajia'_{ij}:=a_{ji}aij′​:=aji​, so that A⊤=(aij′)A^\top = (a'_{ij})A⊤=(aij′​).

Let AAA have the stated properties. Since AAA has less than unit column sums, A⊤A^\topA⊤ has less than unit rows, so A⊤A^\topA⊤ is substochastic.

Now fix m∈[n]m \in \natset{n}m∈[n] and take i∈[n]i \in \natset{n}i∈[n] such that i→mi \to mi→m under AAA and ∑kaki<1\sum_k a_{ki} < 1∑k​aki​<1. By Exercise 1.4.4, i→mi \to mi→m under AAA is equivalent to m→im \to im→i under A⊤A^\topA⊤. Moreover ∑kaki<1\sum_k a_{ki} < 1∑k​aki​<1 is equivalent to ∑kaik′<1\sum_k a'_{ik} < 1∑k​aik′​<1. Hence A⊤A^\topA⊤ is weakly chained substochastic.

Proposition 2.3.5.

For a substochastic matrix PPP, we have

r(P)<1  ⟺  P is weakly chained substochastic.r(P) < 1 \quad \iff \quad P \text{ is weakly chained substochastic}.r(P)<1⟺P is weakly chained substochastic.

A proof can be found in Corollary 2.6 of Azimzadeh (2019).

Now we return to the input output model. Let’s agree to say that sector iii is an upstream supplier to sector jjj if i→ji \to ji→j in the input-output network. By Proposition 1.4.2, an equivalent statement is that there exists a k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N such that aijk>0a^k_{ij} > 0aijk​>0.

Exercise 2.3.23

Let AAA be the adjacency matrix of an input-output network and assume that value added is nonnegative in each sector. Using Proposition 2.3.5, show that r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 if and only if each sector in the network has an upstream supplier with positive value added.

Solution to Exercise 2.3.23

Let AAA be the adjacency matrix of an input-output network such that value added is nonnegative in each sector. In what follows, we write aij′a'_{ij}aij′​ for the i,ji,ji,j-th element of A⊤A^\topA⊤, so that aij′=ajia'_{ij} = a_{ji}aij′​=aji​.

Let’s say that AAA has property U if, for each sector in the network, there exists an upstream supplier with positive value added. Property U is equivalent to the statement that, for all m∈[n]m \in \natset{n}m∈[n], there is an i∈[n]i \in \natset{n}i∈[n] with i→mi \to mi→m under AAA and ∑kaki<1\sum_k a_{ki} < 1∑k​aki​<1. By Exercise 2.3.22, this is equivalent to the statement that A⊤A^\topA⊤ is weakly chained substochastic. Since A⊤A^\topA⊤ is substochastic, this is, in turn equivalent to r(A⊤)<1r(A^\top) < 1r(A⊤)<1. But r(A)=r(A⊤)r(A)=r(A^\top)r(A)=r(A⊤), so property U is equivalent to r(A)<1r(A)<1r(A)<1.

2.3.4.2A Converse to the Neumann Series Lemma¶

Since the Neumann series lemma is a foundational result with many economic applications, we want to know what happens when the conditions of the lemma fail. Here is a partial converse:

Theorem 2.3.6.

Fix A∈Mn×nA \in \matset{n}{n}A∈Mn×n with A⩾0A \geq 0A⩾0. If AAA is irreducible, then the following statements are equivalent:

  1. r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1.

  2. x=Ax+bx = A x + bx=Ax+b has a unique everywhere positive solution for all b⩾0b \geq 0b⩾0 with b≠0b \neq 0b=0.

  3. x=Ax+bx = A x + bx=Ax+b has a nonnegative solution for at least one b⩾0b \geq 0b⩾0 with b≠0b \neq 0b=0.

  4. There exists an x≫0x \gg 0x≫0 such that Ax≪xAx \ll xAx≪x.

Remark 2.3.1.

If AAA is irreducible and one of (and hence all of) items (i)–(iv) are true, then, by the Neumann series lemma, the unique solution is x∗:=∑m⩾0Ambx^* := \sum_{m \geq 0} A^m bx∗:=∑m⩾0​Amb.

Remark 2.3.2.

Statement (iii) is obviously weaker than statement (ii). It is important, however, in the case where r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 fails. In this setting, from the negation of (iii), we can conclude that there is not even one nontrivial bbb in R+n\RR^n_+R+n​ such that a nonnegative solution to x=Ax+bx=Ax+bx=Ax+b exists.

Proof.

Exercise 2.3.25

Irreducibility cannot be dropped from Theorem 2.3.6. Provide an example demonstrating that, without irreducibility, we can have r(A)⩾1r(A) \geq 1r(A)⩾1 for some A⩾0A \geq 0A⩾0 and yet find a nonzero b⩾0b \geq 0b⩾0 and an x⩾0x \geq 0x⩾0 such that x=Ax+bx = A x + bx=Ax+b.

Solution to Exercise 2.3.25

Let A=diag⁡(a,1)A = \diag(a, 1)A=diag(a,1) where 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1. Clearly r(A)=1r(A) = 1r(A)=1. Let b⊤=(1,0)b^\top = (1, 0)b⊤=(1,0) and let x⊤=(1/(1−a),0)x^\top = (1/(1-a), 0)x⊤=(1/(1−a),0). Simple algebra shows that x=Ax+bx = Ax + bx=Ax+b.

2.4Chapter Notes¶

High quality foundational textbooks on input-output analysis and multisector production networks include Nikaido (1968), Miller & Blair (2009) and Antras (2020). References on production networks and aggregate shocks include Acemoglu et al. (2012), Antràs et al. (2012), Di Giovanni et al. (2014), Carvalho (2014), Barrot & Sauvagnat (2016), Baqaee (2018), Carvalho & Tahbaz-Salehi (2019), Acemoglu & Azar (2020), Liu & Tsyvinski (2020), Miranda-Pinto (2021) and Carvalho et al. (2021).

For other network-centric analysis of multisector models, see, for example, Bernard et al. (2019), who use buyer-supplier relationship data from Belgium to investigate the origins of firm size heterogeneity when firms are interconnected in a production network. Herskovic (2018) analyzes asset pricing implications of production networks. Cai & Szeidl (2018) consider the effect of interfirm relationships on business performance. La'O & Tahbaz-Salehi (2022) study optimal monetary policy in a production network. Dew-Becker (2022) analyzes tail risk and aggregate fluctuations in a nonlinear production network. Elliott et al. (2022) show that complex supply networks can greatly amplify small idiosyncratic shocks. Elliott & Golub (2022) provide a survey of network fragility that includes discussion of production networks and the impact of sectoral shocks.
